page.title: Are Lithium Batteries Good for Golf Carts? Yes, With a 200 A BMS
page.h1: Are lithium batteries good for golf carts?
page.desc: Yes, if the pack's BMS keeps up: a loaded cart pulled 168 A on a 12° hill. Vatrer's 200 A 48V kit plus a 12V converter, with the arithmetic.
page.answer: Short answer. Yes, lithium batteries are good for golf carts if the pack's BMS keeps up on hills: Polinovel measured a 168 A peak on a 12° grade with two riders. The Vatrer 48V 105Ah kit (200 A continuous) clears it; add Vatrer's 25 A 48V-to-12V converter for lights.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Hill headroom: Vatrer's 200 A − the 168 A measured peak = 32 A to spare. Redodo states 5,000 W, and 5,000 W ÷ 51.2 V ≈ 98 A, so the same hill asks for 168 ÷ 98 ≈ 1.7× that.
  • Range: LiTime measured 109.73 Wh per mile on a 48V E-Z-GO with one driver. 5,376 Wh ÷ 109.73 ≈ 49 miles for the Vatrer pack, and 5,120 Wh ÷ 109.73 ≈ 46.7 miles for the Redodo.
  • Recharge: 105 Ah ÷ 18 A ≈ 5.8 h on Vatrer's 58.4 V 18 A charger. 100 Ah ÷ 18 A ≈ 5.6 h on Redodo's, which matches Redodo's stated 5.6 h.
  • Weight: Redodo puts its 48V pack at 82 lb against 383 lb for the lead-acid bank it replaces: 383 − 82 = 301 lb off the cart.
  • Cost of the set: $1,579.99 + $79.99 = $1,659.98 at Vatrer today. The Redodo kit costs $1,579.99 − $1,149.99 = $430 less than the Vatrer battery kit.

The kit: Vatrer's 48V 105Ah Club Car conversion kit (battery, dedicated charger, LCD monitor, mounting bracket) plus Vatrer's 25 A / 335 W 48V-to-12V converter, both from Vatrer's own store. {kit:kit-lithium-golf-cart-conversion} EZGO owners can swap in the EZGO version of the same pack at the same price.

Why the BMS amp rating decides whether lithium works

A lithium pack holds its voltage under load, but its battery management system (BMS) shuts it off when current exceeds its limit. U.S. Battery says the BMS "can force a battery to shut down" on steep hills and heavy loads as current draw heats the cells, and its fix is to "add more current-draw capacity instead of Ah capacity".

The cart's controller sets how much current the motor can ask for. The Curtis replacement controller for the 2010-up E-Z-GO TXT 48 is rated 250 A (Buggies Unlimited), and the 2000–2009 Club Car DS/Precedent IQ controller is rated 350 A (FridayParts). In a load test by Polinovel, a battery maker, a cart with two passengers climbing a 12° grade peaked at 168 A. Polinovel says a pack with a 100 A BMS "works on flat ground" and uses 200 A continuous as its own minimum.

Other checks before the swap:

  • Club Car on-board computer (OBC): ImpactBattery says Club Car fitted the OBC to 48V carts "as early as 1995". On 2006-and-newer models a non-OEM charger "will not be able to recognize the voltage" and won't start. ImpactBattery's bypass is a 12-gauge wire from pack negative to the black-wire terminal on the back of the charge receptacle.
  • IQ vs Regen 2: Polinovel calls applying IQ bypass steps to a Regen 2 cart one of the most frequently reported errors, and it leaves the cart unable to move.
  • Charge-port interlock wire: left floating, it tells the controller the charger is still plugged in, which locks out the motor. Polinovel ties it to battery positive.
  • Pre-2010 Club Car DS with a Curtis PMC 1204: a full LiFePO4 pack sits at 58.4 V, which Polinovel says may trip that controller's high-voltage cutoff. The 1204 can't be recalibrated, so it has to be replaced.
  • Regen carts such as the E-Z-GO RXV: hard downhill braking can push charge current past the BMS limit, so the cart cuts power while braking (Polinovel). Either disable regen or confirm the BMS charge-current rating.
  • 12 V accessories: Epoch notes that lead-acid carts were sometimes wired to one 12 V battery in the series bank. A single 48V lithium pack has no 12 V tap, and connecting 12 V accessories directly to a 48V lithium battery "can damage them immediately" (Epoch). The converter in the kit solves this.

Not recommended

Don't build a 48V cart pack from four 12V 100Ah Group 24 lithium batteries in series. Redodo's own listings for its 12V 100Ah Group 24 batteries say they are "NOT suitable for use as a starter battery, golf cart battery, or for high-power applications". Use a single 48V pack built and rated for golf carts.
